title: The New Pump-House, about 1885 (working draft)
method: Working draft, modeled with Claude for Chris Busse from curated parts in tools/stations/pump_house.py: outline from OpenStreetMap; levels from the 2019 schematic design study; machinery from The American Engineer (1884), text and engravings; rooms from the 2002 National Register nomination and HAER VA-34. Every part names its sources and how it is known.
about: Richmond's New Pump-House, 1881-83, by Col. Wilfred Emory Cutshaw: canal water turned three turbines that drove nine pumps, lifting drinking water to the Byrd Park reservoir; an open-air pavilion over the machines held dances and pleasure parties.

epochs.title: The New Pump-House at work
epochs.note: The original Ramsay machinery, two years in service; the pavilion still open.

features.name: The New Pump-House: west wing
features.note: Random-ashlar granite from the site and James Netherwood's quarries, built 1881-83 by Col. Wilfred Emory Cutshaw, city engineer (NRHP 2002). Outline from OpenStreetMap; wall thickness approximate. Each end is a cross-gabled wing with lancet windows, a steep slate roof and pinnacled gables; the upper floor held the gentlemen's powder room and offices, and a stair at the south corner (NRHP 2002). The wing roof's height is scaled from HAER VA-34-1 (approximate).

features.note: The machine room floor: wood in its day, "long removed"; granite and earth today (NRHP 2002). Its two levels are the 2019 study's "Level 1 lower" and "Level 1 upper"; the A-frames stand on the lower, 7 1/2 ft under the shafts (The American Engineer, 1884). Where the one steps up to the other is approximate.

features.name: The New Pump-House: turbine wheel 1
features.note: A partial vertical turbine of the outward-flow (Fourneyron) type, all iron, 21 ft inside and 23 ft outside; water under a 20-ft head came in through its center to a guide chamber that turned it onto about a quarter of the buckets. The American Engineer, December 26, 1884, pp. 260-261: designed by the late Prof. Charles A. Smith, built and erected by H. A. Ramsay (Ramsay Engineering Works, Baltimore) under contract with Col. W. E. Cutshaw. Bolling (1900) gives 23 1/2 ft. Replaced in 1891 by geared Leffel wheels (NRHP 2002; Bolling 1900). Form and size scaled from the engravings, which carry no scale, by the dimensions in the text. Where each gang stood along the room is approximate: no drawing of the room with the machines in it was found.

features.note: A large cast-iron diffuser below the wheel "delivers the water into the tail-race with the least possible loss" (The American Engineer, 1884). 12 ft across and reaching 17 ft under the shaft in the engraving; its flare is drawn square. features.name: The New Pump-House: penstock 1
features.note: An iron penstock 5 ft in diameter, from its sluice gate in the forebay wall down at a slant to an elbow that turns it into the wheel's center (The American Engineer, 1884, pp. 260-261); three openings in the north wall (NRHP 2002; HAER VA-34-5). features.name: Pump House Canal (the forebay)
features.note: The forebay: the Pump House Canal, turned off above the Three Mile Locks and dammed at the east end of the house; its waterline level with the walkway round the north front (NRHP 2002). The channel's banks and bed are today's lidar (3DEP); its 1885 level is inferred, not measured.
